claim: Induced excitatory neurons (iNeurons, iNs) were generated from chimpanzee, bonobo, and human stem cells by expressing the transcription factor neurogenin-2 (NGN2).
source: We generated induced excitatory neurons (iNeurons, iNs) from chimpanzee, bonobo, and human stem cells by expressing the transcription factor neurogenin-2 (NGN2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the methods section describing the generation of rtTA/Ngn2-positive PSC lines.

claim: Genes involved in dendrite and synapse development are expressed earlier during iNs maturation in chimpanzee and bonobo than in human cells.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing showed that genes involved in dendrite and synapse development are expressed earlier during iNs maturation in the chimpanzee and bonobo than the human cells.
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data showing enrichment of dendrite and synapse-related genes at earlier timepoints in ape cells (Figure 4C).

claim: During the first 2 weeks of differentiation, chimpanzee and bonobo iNs showed repetitive action potentials more frequently than human iNs.
source: In accordance, during the first 2 weeks of differentiation, chimpanzee and bonobo iNs showed repetitive action potentials and more spontaneous excitatory activity than human iNs, and extended neurites of higher total length.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing that ape iNs fire repetitive action potentials at d14-16 while human iNs mainly fire single APs (Figure 5A,B).

claim: During the first 2 weeks of differentiation, chimpanzee and bonobo iNs showed more spontaneous excitatory activity than human iNs.
source: In accordance, during the first 2 weeks of differentiation, chimpanzee and bonobo iNs showed repetitive action potentials and more spontaneous excitatory activity than human iNs, and extended neurites of higher total length.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents (sEPSCs) showing ape iNs develop spontaneous activity after 2-3 weeks while human iNs remain mostly silent (Figure 5C,D).

claim: During the first 2 weeks of differentiation, chimpanzee and bonobo iNs extended neurites of higher total length than human iNs.
source: In accordance, during the first 2 weeks of differentiation, chimpanzee and bonobo iNs showed repetitive action potentials and more spontaneous excitatory activity than human iNs, and extended neurites of higher total length.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis showing ape multipolar and bipolar iNs have larger total neurite length at d7 and d14 (Figure 2G,H).

claim: The axons of human iNs were slightly longer at 5 weeks of differentiation compared to ape iNs.
source: However, the axons of human iNs were slightly longer at 5 weeks of differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis showing human multipolar iNs have slightly longer axons at d35 (Figure 2I).

claim: The timing of the establishment of neuronal polarity did not differ between the species.
source: The timing of the establishment of neuronal polarity did not differ between the species.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining showing similar patterns of TUJI and neurofilament colocalization at d7 in both apes and humans (Figure 1E).

claim: Chimpanzee, bonobo, and human neurites eventually reached the same level of structural complexity.
source: Chimpanzee, bonobo, and human neurites eventually reached the same level of structural complexity.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis showing no differences in total neurite length and number of arborizations at d21 and d35 between ape and human iNs.

claim: Human iNs develop slower than chimpanzee and bonobo iNs.
source: Thus, human iNs develop slower than chimpanzee and bonobo iNs, and this difference in timing likely depends on functions downstream of NGN2.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including transcriptional, morphological, and electrophysiological data showing delayed maturation in human iNs.

claim: The difference in timing of neuronal maturation between human and ape iNs likely depends on functions downstream of NGN2.
source: Thus, human iNs develop slower than chimpanzee and bonobo iNs, and this difference in timing likely depends on functions downstream of NGN2.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that NGN2 is exogenously expressed in both species, yet differences in maturation timing are observed, suggesting downstream mechanisms are responsible.

claim: Differences in cognitive abilities between humans and non-human primates are thought to depend on greater numbers of neurons and more complex neural architectures in humans.
source: Differences in cognitive abilities between humans and non-human primates are thought to depend on greater numbers of neurons and more complex neural architectures in humans (Geschwind and Rakic, 2013; Herculano-Houzel, 2012; Smaers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Primate brains contain a greater number of neural stem and progenitor cells that generate neurons compared to other mammals.
source: Compared to other mammals, primate brains contain a greater number of neural stem and progenitor cells that generate neurons (Florio and Huttner, 2014; Borrell and Reillo, 2012; Lui et al., 2011; Smart et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some types of neurons differ structurally among primate species.
source: In addition, some types of neurons differ structurally among primate species (Elston, 2011; DeFelipe, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human cortical pyramidal neurons have longer and more branched dendrites than chimpanzee pyramidal neurons.
source: For example, human cortical pyramidal neurons have longer and more branched dendrites than chimpanzee pyramidal neurons (Bianchi et al., 2013a) and synaptogenesis and development of pyramidal neurons in humans and chimpanzees may be longer than in macaques (Bianchi et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Synaptogenesis and development of pyramidal neurons in humans and chimpanzees may be longer than in macaques.
source: For example, human cortical pyramidal neurons have longer and more branched dendrites than chimpanzee pyramidal neurons (Bianchi et al., 2013a) and synaptogenesis and development of pyramidal neurons in humans and chimpanzees may be longer than in macaques (Bianchi et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A higher degree of connectivity in human neocortex than in other primates could provide a basis for human-specific cognitive abilities.
source: Given the role of pyramidal neurons in higher cognitive functions (Goldman-Rakic, 1999), a higher degree of connectivity in human neocortex than in other primates could provide a basis for human-specific cognitive abilities (DeFelipe, 2011; Bianchi et al., 2013a; Bianchi et al., 2013b; Elston et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human iPSC-derived pyramidal neurons have been found to mature slower than their chimpanzee counterparts both structurally and functionally.
source: Recently, human iPSC-derived pyramidal neurons have been found to mature slower than their chimpanzee counterparts both structurally and functionally and to end up having higher dendrite complexity and spine density (Marchetto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human iPSC-derived pyramidal neurons end up having higher dendrite complexity and spine density than chimpanzee neurons.
source: Recently, human iPSC-derived pyramidal neurons have been found to mature slower than their chimpanzee counterparts both structurally and functionally and to end up having higher dendrite complexity and spine density (Marchetto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon transplantation into the mouse neocortex, human neurons retain juvenile-like dendritic spines dynamics and mature both structurally and functionally over a protracted window of time.
source: In addition, upon transplantation into the mouse neocortex human neurons were shown to retain juvenile-like dendritic spines dynamics and to mature both structurally and functionally over a protracted window of time (Linaro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The human brain develops and matures slower than that of closely related primates.
source: These findings are in line with previous studies suggesting that the human brain develops and matures slower than that of closely related primates (Rakic, 2009; Somel et al., 2009; Charrier et al., 2012; Teffer et al., 2013) and point to the idea that human neurons and human brain develop with different temporal dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NGN2 overexpression allows uncoupling of cell cycle progression of neural progenitors and developmental processes from neuronal maturation.
source: This protocol allows to uncouple cell cycle progression of neural progenitors and developmental processes from neuronal maturation.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of the NGN2 direct conversion system.

claim: The direct conversion paradigm offers a powerful tool to directly study the intrinsic differences in the dynamics of neuronal maturation.
source: It therefore offers a powerful tool to directly study the intrinsic differences in the dynamics of neuronal maturation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the direct conversion system.

claim: A clear delayed maturation of human iNs compared to chimpanzee was observed at the functional and transcriptional level.
source: We followed the temporal differentiation of human and ape induced excitatory neurons (iNeurons, iNs) using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), electrophysiology, and morphological analysis of dendritic arborization, and we observed a clear delayed maturation of human iNs compared to chimpanzee at the functional and transcriptional level.
evidence: This is supported by the scRNAseq and electrophysiology data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The delayed maturation is a cell-intrinsic feature of human neurons.
source: The direct conversion paradigm we used allows us to develop further previous findings by finding evidence for a delayed maturation being a cell-intrinsic feature of human neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the use of the direct conversion system which isolates cell-intrinsic properties from environmental factors.

claim: Unlike previous reports describing iNs as a homogenous population of cortical, upper layer neurons, heterogeneous neuronal cell populations with a majority of cortical sensory neurons were observed.
source: In addition, unlike previous reports describing iNs as a homogenous population of cortical, upper layer neurons, we observed heterogeneous neuronal cell populations with a majority of cortical sensory neurons, further suggesting that the delayed maturation is a general feature of human neurons.
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data showing expression of sensory neuron markers (Figure 3).

claim: The delayed maturation is a general feature of human neurons.
source: In addition, unlike previous reports describing iNs as a homogenous population of cortical, upper layer neurons, we observed heterogeneous neuronal cell populations with a majority of cortical sensory neurons, further suggesting that the delayed maturation is a general feature of human neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that delayed maturation occurs across different neuronal subtypes.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) was performed for one chimpanzee (SandraA) and three human (409B2, SC102A1, and H9) cell lines.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) was performed for one chimpanzee (SandraA) and three human (409B2, SC102A1, and H9) cell lines
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and methods section.

claim: Electrophysiology was performed using all eight cell lines.
source: electrophysiology was performed using all eight cell lines
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend.

claim: Morphological analyses were done with two chimpanzee (SandraA and JoC), the bonobo (BmRNA), and three human (409B2, SC102A1, and H9) cell lines.
source: morphological analyses were done with two chimpanzee (SandraA and JoC), the bonobo (BmRNA), and three human (409B2, SC102A1, and H9) cell lines.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend.

claim: Differentiation was characterized by a downregulation of the stem cell markers NANOG, OCT4, and SOX2 in both ape and human cells.
source: Differentiation was characterized by a downregulation of the stem cell markers NANOG, OCT4, and SOX2 in both ape and human cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data showing reduced expression of stem cell markers.

claim: Neurites were positive for TUJI (beta-III-tubulin, a neuronal marker) starting from d3 of differentiation in apes and humans.
source: Neurites were positive for TUJI (beta-III-tubulin, a neuronal marker) starting from d3 of differentiation in apes and humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing TUJI expression.

claim: By the end of the differentiation at d35, both ape and human cells formed networks that were positive for MAP2 (microtubule associated protein-2, marker for mature neurons) and SYN1 (synapsin-1, synaptic vesicle marker).
source: By the end of the differentiation at d35, both ape and human cells formed networks that were positive for MAP2 (microtubule associated protein-2, marker for mature neurons) and SYN1 (synapsin-1, synaptic vesicle marker; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing MAP2 and SYN1 expression.

claim: The presence of SYN1-positive puncta suggested that the iNs formed synaptic connections.
source: The presence of SYN1-positive puncta suggested that the iNs formed synaptic connections.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of synaptic vesicle markers in punctate patterns.

claim: At d3, TUJI largely colocalizes with neurofilaments, suggesting that the cells were not yet polarized.
source: At d3, TUJI largely colocalizes with neurofilaments, suggesting that the cells were not yet polarized (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, high magnification in panels B and C).
evidence: This is inferred from immunostaining data showing colocalization patterns.

claim: At d7, the degree of colocalization between TUJI and neurofilament markers decreased, suggesting that the iNs established axo-dendritic polarity.
source: At d7, the degree of colocalization between TUJI and neurofilament markers decreased, suggesting that the iNs established axo-dendritic polarity (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from immunostaining data showing decreased colocalization.

claim: The pattern of staining of the cytoskeletal components did not differ between apes and humans, suggesting that the timing of axo-dendritic polarity establishment is similar.
source: The pattern of staining of the cytoskeletal components did not differ between apes and humans, suggesting that the timing of axo-dendritic polarity establishment is similar.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both species show similar staining patterns at the same timepoints.

claim: The majority of iNs (25/26 cells) had a single axon.
source: The majority of iNs (25/26 cells) had a single axon, which is in line with previous findings (Rhee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by sparse labeling and tracing of individual cells.

claim: The axon was always the longest neurite and was positive for the axonal marker (n = 26 cells).
source: In addition, it was always the longest neurite, which was found to be positive for the axonal marker (n = 26 cells, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and morphological analysis.

claim: For both apes and humans, unipolar, bipolar, and multipolar iNs were observed at all time points analyzed.
source: For both apes and humans, unipolar, bipolar, and multipolar iNs were observed at all time points analyzed (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis of traced neurons.

claim: For the apes, 69% of neurons were multipolar, 26% bipolar, and 5% unipolar.
source: For the apes and humans, 69% and 58% of neurons were multipolar, 26% and 36% bipolar, and 5% and 7% unipolar, respectively (% of all neurons from all time points).
evidence: This is based on quantification of traced neurons across all timepoints.

claim: For humans, 58% of neurons were multipolar, 36% bipolar, and 7% unipolar.
source: For the apes and humans, 69% and 58% of neurons were multipolar, 26% and 36% bipolar, and 5% and 7% unipolar, respectively (% of all neurons from all time points).
evidence: This is based on quantification of traced neurons across all timepoints.

claim: At d7 and d14 of differentiation, ape multipolar iNs have neurite trees of larger total length than human multipolar iNs.
source: At d7 and d14 of differentiation, ape multipolar (Figure 2G; pd7 = 0.0098; pd14 = 0.0215 Mann–Whitney U test) and bipolar (Figure 2H; pd7 = 0.0278; pd14 <0.001 Mann–Whitney U test) iNs have neurite trees of larger total length.
evidence: This is supported by morphological quantification showing statistically significant differences.

claim: At d7 and d14 of differentiation, ape bipolar iNs have neurite trees of larger total length than human bipolar iNs.
source: At d7 and d14 of differentiation, ape multipolar (Figure 2G; pd7 = 0.0098; pd14 = 0.0215 Mann–Whitney U test) and bipolar (Figure 2H; pd7 = 0.0278; pd14 <0.001 Mann–Whitney U test) iNs have neurite trees of larger total length.
evidence: This is supported by morphological quantification showing statistically significant differences.

claim: At d14, ape cells have more Sholl intersections than human cells for both multipolar and bipolar iNs.
source: At d14, ape cells have more Sholl intersections (intersections of neurites with concentric circles around the cell body) than human cells (Figure 2K; pmultipolar = 0.0469; Figure 2L; pbipolar < 0.001 Mann–Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by morphological quantification showing statistically significant differences.

claim: At early stages of maturation ape iNs have larger neurite trees than human iNs.
source: Thus, at early stages of maturation ape, iNs have larger neurite trees than human iNs.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the morphological data at d7 and d14.

claim: At later time points (d21 and d35), total neurite length and number of arborizations did not differ between ape and human iNs.
source: At later time points (d21 and d35), total neurite length and number of arborizations did not differ between ape and human iNs.
evidence: This is based on morphological quantification showing no significant differences at these timepoints.

claim: Human multipolar iNs have slightly longer axons at d35 of differentiation compared to ape iNs.
source: Human multipolar iNs have slightly longer axons (the longest neurite) at d35 of differentiation compared to ape iNs (Figure 2I; pd35 = 0.0094 Mann–Whitney U test)
evidence: This is supported by morphological quantification showing statistically significant differences.

claim: For other neurites (excluding the longest ones), human neurons have longer total neurite length at d14 of differentiation.
source: whereas for other neurites (excluding the longest ones), human neurons have longer total neurite length at d14 of differentiation (Figure 2M; pmultipolar = 0.0009; Figure 2N; pbipolar = 0.447, unpaired T-test), but show no difference at d21 and d35.
evidence: This is supported by morphological quantification showing statistically significant differences for multipolar iNs.

claim: After data processing, 10,111 ape and 25,923 human iNs were retained across the four time points.
source: After data processing, we retained 10,111 ape and 25,923 human iNs across the four time points (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing scRNAseq data processing.

claim: Unsupervised clustering analysis of the combined datasets identified eight clusters of cells based on gene expression patterns.
source: Unsupervised clustering analysis of the combined datasets identified eight clusters of cells based on gene expression patterns (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Ape and human cells occurred in all clusters, albeit at different proportions.
source: Ape and human cells occurred in all clusters, albeit at different proportions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of scRNAseq data showing species distribution across clusters.

claim: Progenitor and neuronal cell populations were identified by SOX2 and MAP2 expression, respectively.
source: Progenitor and neuronal cell populations were identified by SOX2 and MAP2 expression, respectively.
evidence: This is based on known marker genes for these cell types.

claim: The cortical markers CUX1 and BRN2 were expressed in both cells expressing progenitor markers and neuronal markers.
source: The cortical markers CUX1 and BRN2 (Figure 3C) were expressed in both cells expressing progenitor markers and neuronal markers.
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data showing marker expression patterns.

claim: Other cortical markers such as SATB2, TBR1, or CTIP2 were detected in a few cells or not detected.
source: Other cortical markers such as SATB2, TBR1, or CTIP2 were detected in a few cells or not detected.
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data showing low or absent expression of these markers.

claim: The clusters include three types of neuronal cells: cells expressing progenitor markers (NP: SOX2+, VIM+, TOP2A+, etc., clusters 1 and 2), intermediate cells (expressing both progenitor and neuronal genes, cluster 3), and neurons (MAP2, SYT1, GAP43, etc., clusters 4, 5, 6, and 7).
source: The clusters include three types of neuronal cells: cells expressing progenitor markers (NP: SOX2+, VIM+, TOP2A+, etc., clusters 1 and 2), intermediate cells (expressing both progenitor and neuronal genes, cluster 3), and neurons (MAP2, SYT1, GAP43, etc., clusters 4, 5, 6, and 7).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: One fibroblast cluster was identified (COL1A1+ and TAGLN+, etc., cluster 8).
source: One fibroblast cluster was also identified (COL1A1+ and TAGLN+, etc., cluster 8) (Figure 3B–C and E).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Three sub-populations of neurons were identified by differential expression of TAC1 (cluster 5), SSTR2 and GAL (cluster 6), and PIEZO and GAL (cluster 7).
source: We could identify three sub-populations of neurons, by differential expression of TAC1 (cluster 5), SSTR2 and GAL (cluster 6), and PIEZO and GAL (cluster 7, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: All three sub-classes of neurons were present in similar proportions for all cell lines and species at all time points of iN differentiation.
source: All three sub-classes were present in similar proportions for all cell lines and species at all time points of iN differentiation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell proportions from scRNAseq data.

claim: The NGN2-induced generation of cells expressing progenitor markers and differentiated neurons is in line with previous findings.
source: The NGN2-induced generation of cells expressing progenitor markers and differentiated neurons is in line with previous findings (Nehme et al., 2018) and with what has been reported for ASCL1-induced neuronal cell populations (Treutlein et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Based on scRNAseq of the neurons, 54.6% (d5) - 35.4% (d35) ape cells were identified as sensory neurons.
source: Based on scRNAseq of the neurons, 54.6% (d5) - 35.4% (d35) ape cells and 80.8% (d5) - 34.3% (d35) human cells were identified as sensory neurons (SNs), when assessed by the expression of the sensory neurons markers PRPH (intermediate neurofilament peripherin), neurotrophin receptor tyrosine receptor kinase B (TRKB, encoded by NTRK2), and homeodomain transcription factors (POU4F1/BRN3A) and PHOX2B (Figure 3F; D'Autréaux et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Based on scRNAseq of the neurons, 80.8% (d5) - 34.3% (d35) human cells were identified as sensory neurons.
source: Based on scRNAseq of the neurons, 54.6% (d5) - 35.4% (d35) ape cells and 80.8% (d5) - 34.3% (d35) human cells were identified as sensory neurons (SNs), when assessed by the expression of the sensory neurons markers PRPH (intermediate neurofilament peripherin), neurotrophin receptor tyrosine receptor kinase B (TRKB, encoded by NTRK2), and homeodomain transcription factors (POU4F1/BRN3A) and PHOX2B (Figure 3F; D'Autréaux et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: NGN2 can induce the differentiation of PSCs into nociceptive sensory neurons.
source: Thus, NGN2 can induce the differentiation of PSCs also into nociceptive sensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of sensory neuron markers and nociceptive markers in the scRNAseq data.

claim: From d5 to d35, 47.1% ape and 38.8% human iNs express VGLUT2 (glutamate transporter).
source: From d5 to d35, 47.1% ape and 38.8% human iNs express VGLUT2 (glutamate transporter; Figure 3F)
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data showing marker expression.

claim: Glutamate decarboxylases (GAD1/2, a marker for GABA-ergic cells) is not detected or expressed lowly in either ape or human iNs, suggesting that the iNs are glutamatergic.
source: while glutamate decarboxylases (GAD1/2, a marker for GABA-ergic cells) is not detected or expressed lowly in either ape or human iNs, suggesting that the iNs are glutamatergic (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence or low expression of GABAergic markers in scRNAseq data.

claim: 35% (BRN2) to 45% (CUX1) of ape neurons express cortical markers.
source: Besides expression of sensory markers, we found that 35% (BRN2) to 45% (CUX1) of ape and 18% (BRN2) to 27% (CUX1) of human neurons express cortical markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data showing marker expression.

claim: 18% (BRN2) to 27% (CUX1) of human neurons express cortical markers.
source: Besides expression of sensory markers, we found that 35% (BRN2) to 45% (CUX1) of ape and 18% (BRN2) to 27% (CUX1) of human neurons express cortical markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data showing marker expression.

claim: 13% (BRN2) to 21% (CUX1) of ape and human neurons express both sensory (PRHP) and cortical markers (BRN2 or CUX1).
source: Thirteen percentage (BRN2) to 21% (CUX1) of ape and human neurons express both sensory (PRHP) and cortical markers (BRN2 or CUX1).
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data showing co-expression of markers.

claim: 8% (BRN2) to 14% (CUX1) of neurons express both sensory (ISL1) and cortical markers, suggesting that a subset of neurons might be sensory neurons of the cortex.
source: scRNAseq data show that 8% (BRN2) to 14% (CUX1) of neurons express both sensory (ISL1) and cortical markers, suggesting that a subset of neurons might be sensory neurons of the cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from scRNAseq data showing co-expression of sensory and cortical markers.

claim: The same cell populations were found in apes and humans, albeit at different proportions, suggesting that NGN2 induces similar neuronal fates in both species.
source: In spite of the heterogeneity of the cultures (see also Lin, 2020), the same cell populations were found in apes and humans, albeit at different proportions, suggesting that NGN2 induces similar neuronal fates in both species.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all identified cell types are present in both species.

claim: Only minor proportions (circa 12%) of iNs were found to be positive for Peripherin (PRPH), a marker for peripheral neurons.
source: In our hands, only minor proportions (circa 12%) of iNs were found to be positive for Peripherin (PRPH), a marker for peripheral neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: iNs were negative for TBR1.
source: iNs were negative for TBR1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data.

claim: 90% of the iNs were positive for CUX1.
source: Ninety percentage of the iNs were positive for CUX1, and 50–60% were positive for BRN2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: 50-60% of iNs were positive for BRN2.
source: Ninety percentage of the iNs were positive for CUX1, and 50–60% were positive for BRN2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: No significant preference for a given cell type was observed between the species.
source: Of note, we did not observe any significant preference for a given cell type between the species (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data.

claim: The vast majority of iNs are upper layers (layers II–IV) cortical neurons in both apes and humans.
source: In line with previous reports (Zhang et al., 2013; Frega et al., 2017), our immunocytochemical data suggest that the vast majority of iNs are upper layers (layers II–IV) cortical neurons in both apes and humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the high percentage of CUX1-positive cells and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 60% of the iNs were positive for ISLET1 at d21 and d35.
source: 60% of the iNs were positive for ISLET1 at d21 and d35 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A)
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: 60-65% of iNs were positive for NAV1.7 at d21.
source: and 60–65% were positive for NAV1.7 at d21 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), with no difference observed between apes and humans.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: A substantial proportion of iNs are cortical sensory neurons.
source: Given that 95% of iNs are positive for CUX1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and previous paragraph), we conclude that a substantial proportion of iNs are cortical sensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-expression of cortical and sensory markers.

claim: A proportion of iNs co-express BRN2 and ISLET1 at the mRNA and protein level at d21 and d35.
source: In line with that, we showed that a proportion of iNs co-express BRN2 and ISLET1 (at the mRNA and protein level, at d21 and d35, see Figure 3—figure supplement 5A)
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The smaller population of sensory iNs not expressing cortical markers is likely to be a population of nociceptive peripheral neurons.
source: The smaller population of sensory iNs not expressing cortical markers is likely to be a population of nociceptive peripheral neurons (Lin, 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression patterns and supported by citation.

claim: iNs are mainly cortical sensory neurons.
source: In summary, based on marker expression at the mRNA and protein level, we conclude that iNs are mainly cortical sensory neurons (for a detailed definition of the criteria we adopted, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of marker expression data.

claim: The same populations are present in similar proportions in apes and humans.
source: Furthermore, the same populations are present in similar proportions in apes and humans (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5), suggesting that NGN2 induces heterogeneous, yet similar fates in all cell lines and species we analyzed.
evidence: This is based on quantification of marker-positive cells showing no significant differences between species.

claim: NGN2 induces heterogeneous, yet similar fates in all cell lines and species analyzed.
source: Furthermore, the same populations are present in similar proportions in apes and humans (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5), suggesting that NGN2 induces heterogeneous, yet similar fates in all cell lines and species we analyzed.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cell type proportions are similar across species.

claim: The human iNs showed similar numbers of higher expressed genes across the different time points.
source: The human iNs showed similar numbers of higher expressed genes across the different time points.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: In contrast to the human iNs, the numbers of higher expressed genes observed in ape iNs varied across the time points.
source: In contrast to the human iNs, the numbers of higher expressed genes observed in ape iNs varied across the time points.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Among the iNs sub-clusters of the same species, similar numbers of higher expressed genes were observed at each time point.
source: Among the iNs sub-clusters of the same species, we observed similar numbers of higher expressed genes at each time point (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Genes involved in axonogenesis (GO: 0007409) and axon guidance (GO: 0007411) are enriched (p<0.04, binomial test) in both ape and human iNs sub-clusters from d5, although more strongly in the apes.
source: Genes involved in axonogenesis (GO: 0007409) and axon guidance (GO: 0007411) are enriched (p<0.04, binomial test) in both ape and human iNs sub-clusters from d5, although more strongly in the apes (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Genes in dendrite development (GO: 0016358) and dendrite morphogenesis (GO: 0048813) are enriched (p<0.05, binomial test) from d5 in the apes, but not in humans.
source: Genes in dendrite development (GO: 0016358) and dendrite morphogenesis (GO: 0048813) are enriched (p<0.05, binomial test) from d5 in the apes, but not in humans (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Genes involved in synapse organization (GO: 0050808) are enriched from d5 in all ape iNs sub-clusters (p<0.03) and become so from d14 in the human iNs (p<0.02, binomial test).
source: Also, genes involved in synapse organization (GO: 0050808) are enriched from d5 in all ape iNs sub-clusters (p<0.03) and become so from d14 in the human iNs (p<0.02, binomial test) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Genes affecting ion transmembrane transport (GO: 0034220) are enriched from d14 in all ape iNs sub-clusters (p<0.03) but do not become enriched even in d35 human iNs (p>0.33, binomial test).
source: In addition, genes affecting ion transmembrane transport (GO: 0034220) are enriched from d14 in all ape iNs sub-clusters (p<0.03) but do not become enriched even in d35 human iNs (p>0.33, binomial test).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Genes affecting axo−dendritic transport (GO: 0008088) and neurotransmitter secretion (GO: 0007269) are more enriched in ape iNs sub-clusters from d5 and d14, respectively.
source: Genes affecting axo−dendritic transport (GO: 0008088) and neurotransmitter secretion (GO: 0007269) are more enriched in ape iNs sub-clusters from d5 and d14, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Neuron-expressed genes involved in synaptic organization, pre-synaptic process, and trans-synaptic signaling (FDR < 0.05, Fisher exact test) started to be expressed in ape iNs from d5 but only from d14 and d28 in human iNs.
source: In agreement with the results using Gene Ontology, neuron-expressed genes involved in synaptic organization, pre-synaptic process, and trans-synaptic signaling (FDR < 0.05, Fisher exact test) started to be expressed in ape iNs from d5 but only from d14 and d28 in human iNs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on SynGO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Most of the groups of genes involved in post-synaptic process and trans-synaptic signaling were not enriched in human iNs for all time points, while they were enriched in ape iNs from d14 onwards.
source: Most of the groups of genes involved in post-synaptic process and trans-synaptic signaling were not enriched in human iNs for all time points, while they were enriched in ape iNs from d14 onwards (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on SynGO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Most of the groups of genes involved in post-synaptic process were enriched in ape iNs from d14 onwards and became so in human iNs at d35.
source: In line with the findings in Figure 4E, most of the groups of genes involved in post-synaptic process were enriched in ape iNs from d14 onwards and became so in human iNs at d35 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SynGO enrichment analysis of conserved differentially expressed genes.

claim: The differences between apes and humans are more obvious at early time points.
source: Of note, the differences between apes and humans are more obvious at early time points.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that enrichment differences are strongest at d5 and d14.

claim: Synaptic gene expression was not enriched in ape or human cells expressing progenitor markers when compared to undifferentiated iPSCs.
source: Synaptic gene expression was not enriched in ape or human cells expressing progenitor markers when compared to undifferentiated iPSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that these changes are not caused by NGN2 expression per se but as part of the induced neuronal maturation.
evidence: This is based on SynGO enrichment analysis comparing progenitors to iPSCs.

claim: The synaptic gene expression changes are not caused by NGN2 expression per se but as part of the induced neuronal maturation.
source: Synaptic gene expression was not enriched in ape or human cells expressing progenitor markers when compared to undifferentiated iPSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that these changes are not caused by NGN2 expression per se but as part of the induced neuronal maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that synaptic genes are not enriched in progenitors which also express NGN2.

claim: After NGN2 induction, genes associated with dendrites and synapses become prominently expressed later in human iNs than in ape iNs.
source: Thus, after NGN2 induction, genes associated with dendrites and synapses become prominently expressed later in human iNs than in ape iNs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the GO and SynGO enrichment analyses.

claim: Vrmp was stable over time and similar between species.
source: Vrmp was stable over time and similar between species (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; d2 - d > 49, two-way Anova (2WA) pday=0.44; pspec=0.78; pday*spec=0.051).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Rcell only increased over the very first days of differentiation and then decreased over time as expected from maturing neuronal cells.
source: Rcell only increased over the very first days of differentiation and then decreased over time as expected from maturing neuronal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) with little differences between ape and human (2WA: pday=1.8E-13; pspec=0.18; pday*spec=0.23).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Ccell increased over time.
source: As expected, Ccell increased over time (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: While the increase in Ccell occurred to a similar extent in both groups from about 20 pF–30 pF and above, the human cells were always slightly but significantly lower than the apes.
source: While the increase occurred to a similar extent in both groups from about 20 pF–30 pF and above, the human cells were always slightly but significantly lower than the apes. (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; 2WA: pday=7.45E-21; pspec=0.02; pday*spec=0.12).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The resulting time constant R*C of the cells were comparatively stable at about 16 ms (ape: 17.4 ms, human: 15.3 ms) and similar to values previously reported for human (or other) neuronal cells.
source: The resulting time constant R*C of the cells were comparatively stable at about 16 ms (ape: 17.4 ms, human: 15.3 ms) and similar to values previously reported for human (or other) neuronal cells (Eyal et al., 2016; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements and comparison to literature values.

claim: Mainly at d14–16, the ape cells had higher time constant values than the human cells mainly due to their high Rcell and low Ccell, respectively.
source: However, mainly at d14–16, the ape cells had higher values than the human cells mainly due to their high Rcell and low Ccell, respectively (2WA: pday=0,17; pspec=0.08; pday*spec=0.023)
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The differentiation of ape and human iNs is accompanied by maturation of their basic electrical properties in a way consistent with what has been observed for other in vitro and in vivo neuronal systems.
source: Thus, the differentiation of ape and human iNs is accompanied by maturation of their basic electrical properties in a way consistent with what has been observed for other in vitro and in vivo neuronal systems (Moody and Bosma, 2005).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Upon induced depolarization, iNs showed single action potentials (APs) as early as day 2 (d2) of differentiation albeit with peak voltages hardly crossing 0 mV.
source: Using the whole-cell current-clamp technique, we found that upon induced depolarization, iNs showed single action potentials (APs) as early as day 2 (d2) of differentiation albeit with peak voltages hardly crossing 0 mV (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Ape iNs showed repetitive action potentials robustly already at d14–16, with its maximal medial frequency increasing slightly over differentiation time.
source: Ape iNs showed repetitive action potentials robustly already at d14–16, with its maximal medial frequency increasing slightly over differentiation time (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Upon induced depolarization, human iNs fired mainly single APs until d21, after which the ability to maintain repetitive firing became established also in the human lines.
source: In contrast, upon induced depolarization, human iNs fired mainly single APs until d21, after which the ability to maintain repetitive firing became established also in the human lines (Figure 5A,B; 2WA: pday=1.98E-24; pspec=2.96E-6; pday*spec=0.15; n=144 ape/156 human iNs).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: mRNAs for sodium, potassium, and calcium channels are expressed in both ape and human iNs, with no species-specific differences.
source: scRNAseq analysis revealed that mRNAs for sodium, potassium, and calcium channels are expressed in both ape and human iNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), with no species-specific differences.
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data showing channel gene expression.

claim: The ape iNs developed spontaneous activity after 2–3 weeks of differentiation.
source: The ape iNs developed spontaneous activity after 2–3 weeks of differentiation.
evidence: This is based on measurements of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents.

claim: The majority of human iNs were silent at 2-3 weeks of differentiation.
source: In contrast, the majority of human iNs were silent at these times (Figure 5C,D; 2WA: pday=0.053; pspec=0.0035; pday*spec=0.071; n = 132 ape/135 human iNs; see Supplementary file 3 for details).
evidence: This is based on measurements of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents and statistical analysis.

claim: sEPSCs became frequent in human iNs only after 3–4 weeks.
source: sEPSCs became frequent in human iNs only after 3–4 weeks.
evidence: This is based on measurements of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents.

claim: Before d14, no spontaneous synaptic activity was observed.
source: Before d14, we did not observe any spontaneous synaptic activity.
evidence: This is based on measurements of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents.

claim: NGN2 expression induces not only cortical fate but also sensory fate in both apes and humans.
source: We confirm and extend previous findings by showing here that NGN2 expression induces not only cortical fate (Zhang et al., 2013; Frega et al., 2017), but also sensory fate in both apes and humans.
evidence: This is based on marker expression data from scRNAseq and immunofluorescence.

claim: Human iNs mature slower than ape iNs from a structural, transcriptional, and functional point of view.
source: Furthermore, we find that human iNs mature slower than ape iNs from a structural, transcriptional, and functional point of view.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: NGN2 induces heterogeneous, yet similar fates in ape and human iNs.
source: A surprising finding in our study was that NGN2 induces heterogeneous, yet similar fates in ape and human iNs.
evidence: This is based on the observation that multiple cell types are present in similar proportions in both species.

claim: The heterogeneity of iNs cultures in human has been so far under-estimated and was recently revealed using the power and resolution of scRNAseq.
source: The heterogeneity of iNs cultures in human has been so far under-estimated and was recently revealed using the power and resolution of scRNAseq (Lin, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The heterogeneity can be beneficial for basic research in evolutionary neurobiology, as it allows modeling in a dish several neuronal fates and features.
source: However, the heterogeneity can be beneficial for basic research in evolutionary neurobiology, as it allows modeling in a dish several neuronal fates and features, of which only a few are expected to show an evolutionary-relevant difference.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential benefits of heterogeneity.

claim: The comparison of different neuronal fates maturing in the same dish offers a valuable internal control when looking for features shared by different cell types.
source: In addition, the comparison of different neuronal fates maturing in the same dish offers a valuable internal control when looking for features shared by different cell types that can in turn be regarded as core components/biological processes showing relevant changes between species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the methodological advantages of heterogeneity.

claim: The use of iNs allows to uncouple early developmental events such as cell cycle progression, proliferation, and differentiation from the intrinsic neuronal maturation properties.
source: Despite its possible limitations, the use of iNs allows to uncouple early developmental events such as cell cycle progression, proliferation, and differentiation from the intrinsic neuronal maturation properties, thus offering the unique opportunity to directly study the cell-intrinsic and evolutionary aspects of neuronal maturation.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of the direct conversion system.

claim: Several fundamental properties of neurons, for example the establishment of axo-dendritic polarity, onset of expression of voltage-gated channels, and basic electrical properties, show little or no differences between apes and humans.
source: Our data show that several fundamental properties of neurons, for example the establishment of axo-dendritic polarity, onset of expression of voltage-gated channels, and basic electrical properties, show little or no differences between apes and humans.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the electrophysiological and morphological data.

claim: Synapse-associated genes become expressed later in human neurons.
source: However, synapse-associated genes become expressed later in human neurons and electrical activity within cells (APs) and between cells (sEPSCs) appear later in the human neurons.
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq and electrophysiology data.

claim: Electrical activity within cells (APs) and between cells (sEPSCs) appear later in the human neurons.
source: However, synapse-associated genes become expressed later in human neurons and electrical activity within cells (APs) and between cells (sEPSCs) appear later in the human neurons.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data.

claim: Comparisons of human, chimpanzee, and macaque post-mortem brains have shown that expression changes of genes associated with synaptic functions and spine formation occur later in humans than in the other primates.
source: In line with that, comparisons of human, chimpanzee, and macaque post-mortem brains have shown that expression changes of genes associated with synaptic functions and spine formation occur later in humans than in the other primates (Lui et al., 2011; Somel et al., 2009; Charrier et al., 2012; Petanjek et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: iNs morphological maturation follows a similar pattern where until d14 post-induction ape neurons have more complex and longer neurites, a difference that disappears by d21.
source: iNs morphological maturation follows a similar pattern where until d14 post-induction ape neurons have more complex and longer neurites, a difference that disappears by d21.
evidence: This is based on morphological quantification data.

claim: A slower neuronal development of neuronal gene expression in humans than in apes has been previously described in organoids and at the organ level.
source: A slower neuronal development of neuronal gene expression in humans than in apes has been previously described in organoids and at the organ level (Kanton et al., 2019; Somel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The data using the iN direct conversion protocol show that the later onset of neuron differentiation and maturation does not only occur in whole organs or complex differentiation systems but happens also in cortical sensory neurons as a downstream effect of NGN2-induced differentiation.
source: Our data using the iN direct conversion protocol show that the later onset of neuron differentiation and maturation does not only occur in whole organs or complex differentiation systems but happens also in cortical sensory neurons as a downstream effect of NGN2-induced differentiation, strongly suggesting that the delayed maturation is a cell-intrinsic property of human neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that delayed maturation occurs in the direct conversion system which isolates cell-intrinsic properties.

claim: The delayed maturation is a cell-intrinsic property of human neurons.
source: Our data using the iN direct conversion protocol show that the later onset of neuron differentiation and maturation does not only occur in whole organs or complex differentiation systems but happens also in cortical sensory neurons as a downstream effect of NGN2-induced differentiation, strongly suggesting that the delayed maturation is a cell-intrinsic property of human neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the use of the direct conversion system.

claim: Sensory neurons are interesting from an evolutionary point of view, as the development and evolution of working memory in human is linked to a higher integration of sensory functions in the human prefrontal cortex.
source: Of note, sensory neurons are interesting from an evolutionary point of view, as the development and evolution of working memory in human is linked to a higher integration of sensory functions in the human prefrontal cortex (Smaers et al., 2017; Lara and Wallis, 2015; Semendeferi et al., 2001; Carlén, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The maturation of synaptic contacts and communication might be driven by two different mechanisms: a transcriptional driver at early time points, setting iNs apart transcriptionally and morphologically, and a post-transcriptional driver at later time points, setting iNs apart functionally.
source: This suggests to us that the maturation of synaptic contacts and communication might be driven by two different mechanisms: a transcriptional driver at early time points, setting iNs apart transcriptionally and morphologically, and a post-transcriptional driver at later time points, setting iNs apart functionally.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that transcriptional differences are milder at later timepoints while functional differences remain dramatic.

claim: An activity-dependent transcriptional and translational regulation might contribute and possibly amplify the differences between ape and human neuronal maturation at the functional level.
source: In addition, an activity-dependent transcriptional and translational regulation (Ghiani et al., 2007; Buffington et al., 2014) might contribute and possibly amplify the differences between ape and human neuronal maturation at the functional level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A possible driver for the differences in neuronal maturation is Slit-Robo Rho GTPase activating protein 2 (SRGAP2).
source: At the molecular level, a possible driver for such differences is Slit-Robo Rho GTPase activating protein 2 (SRGAP2) (Charrier et al., 2012), wherein three duplication events have occurred on the modern human lineage (Dennis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Expression of the human-specific form SRGAP2C variant leads to neoteny in spine maturation and might contribute to human brain evolution.
source: Expression of the human-specific form SRGAP2C variant leads to neoteny in spine maturation and might contribute to human brain evolution (Charrier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The later onset of neurite outgrowth has been speculated to result in more complex dendritic trees.
source: The delayed development and maturation of human neurons may have several possible consequences for the organization and function in the adult brain. The later onset of neurite outgrowth shown here and by others (Otani et al., 2016; Marchetto et al., 2019; Petanjek et al., 2011; Linaro et al., 2019) has been speculated to result in more complex dendritic trees (Bianchi et al., 2013a; Elston et al., 2001; Marchetto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At d35, the axons of the human multipolar neurons are slightly longer than in the ape neurons.
source: Interestingly, at d35, we find that the axons of the human multipolar neurons are slightly longer than in the ape neurons.
evidence: This is based on morphological quantification data.

claim: Longer axons would make contacts over greater distances in the brain possible.
source: Of note, longer axons would obviously make contacts over greater distances in the brain possible.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between axon length and connectivity.

claim: Since the human brain is three times bigger than the ape brains, axons may be longer in human brains than in ape brains and that may affect the extent of neuronal projections in human brains.
source: Since the human brain is three times bigger than the ape brains, in the future it will be interesting to investigate whether axons may be longer in human brains than in ape brains and whether that may affect the extent of neuronal projections in human brains.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.
